"Dispense with something" means to choose not to use something, or to get rid of something, often because it is unnecessary, inconvenient, or no longer needed.

Think of it this way: you are removing something from the picture — a rule, a step, a formality, a person, or a habit — and deciding to move forward without it.
Why This Phrase Can Be Confusing

Many learners stumble here because the word "dispense" on its own means something very different. A pharmacy dispenses medicine — meaning it gives out or distributes medicine. A vending machine dispenses snacks — it delivers them to you.

But the moment you add "with," the entire meaning flips:

  • Dispense = to give out or distribute something
  • Dispense with = to do away with something; to go without it

This is the power of phrasal verbs in English — a small word like "with" can completely transform the meaning. So always treat "dispense with" as a single, inseparable unit.
The Three Closely Related Meanings

Meaning 1: To decide to skip or omit something

This is the most common use. You choose not to bother with something — especially something that is normally expected or traditionally included — because you want to save time, simplify things, or because it feels unnecessary.

Examples:

  • "Let's dispense with the introductions and get straight to work."
    (= Let's skip the introductions.)
  • "She decided to dispense with a wedding ceremony and simply sign the papers."
    (= She chose not to have a ceremony.)
  • "The judge dispensed with the usual procedures given the emergency."
    (= The judge skipped the usual procedures.)

In all these cases, something that normally happens is being left out on purpose.

Meaning 2: To get rid of something permanently

Here, you are eliminating something that was previously in use — abolishing it, removing it from practice, or stopping its use altogether.

Examples:

  • "The new manager dispensed with the old filing system."
    (= The manager got rid of the old filing system entirely.)
  • "The company dispensed with several outdated rules."
    (= The company abolished those rules.)
  • "They dispensed with the use of paper forms and moved everything online."
    (= They permanently stopped using paper forms.)

The difference from Meaning 1 is subtle but real. In Meaning 1, you're skipping something in a specific moment. In Meaning 2, you are permanently eliminating something from regular practice.

Meaning 3: To dismiss or release a person from service (formal)

This is a polite, formal — and sometimes euphemistic — way of saying that someone's employment or services are being ended or terminated. It is often used in professional or legal contexts.

Examples:

  • "The firm dispensed with his services after the project was completed."
    (= The firm let him go / terminated his contract.)
  • "They dispensed with the consultant once a permanent employee was hired."
    (= They no longer needed the consultant's services.)

This meaning is used when the speaker wants to sound professional or avoid blunt language like "fired" or "dismissed."
The Feeling Behind the Idiom

Across all three meanings, there is a common emotional thread: the idea that something is being actively set aside, removed, or bypassed — usually because it is seen as:

  • Unnecessary
  • A waste of time
  • Outdated or no longer useful
  • Inconvenient in the current situation

It carries a sense of decisiveness. When someone dispenses with something, they are making a deliberate, confident choice to move forward without it.
Grammar: How to Use It Correctly

"Dispense with" is a phrasal verb, and it always takes an object — meaning something must always follow "with." You cannot use "dispense with" and leave it hanging.

✅ Correct:

  • "Let's dispense with the rules for today."
  • "She dispensed with formality and called him by his first name."

❌ Incorrect:

  • "Let's dispense with." (no object — incomplete)

Also, you cannot separate this phrasal verb. The word "with" must always stay attached.

❌ Incorrect: "Let's dispense the formalities with."
✅ Correct: "Let's dispense with the formalities."
Tone and Register

This phrase leans slightly formal. You will hear it most often in:

  • Professional settings (business meetings, workplaces)
  • Legal or official contexts
  • Formal writing
  • Situations where the speaker wants to sound decisive and in control

In casual conversation, people might instead say "skip it," "forget about it," "do without it," or "get rid of it." But "dispense with" adds a layer of polish and authority that those alternatives don't always carry.
Common Real-Life Situations

SituationHow the Idiom Fits

Here are common real-life situations where you'd naturally encounter or use this idiom:

In a meeting: "Let's dispense with the small talk and focus on the agenda."

In a law or government context: "The court dispensed with certain procedural requirements in the interest of time."

In a restaurant or personal habit: "He dispensed with dessert and went straight for coffee."

In describing social behavior: "She dispensed with pleasantries and asked him directly what he wanted."

In business decisions: "The startup dispensed with traditional office hours and let employees work flexibly."
Synonyms — Words With a Similar Meaning

Depending on the context, you can often replace "dispense with" with:

  • Do without (most natural in everyday speech)
  • Forgo (formal; to willingly give something up)
  • Skip (casual; to omit something)
  • Omit (to leave something out)
  • Drop (to stop using something)
  • Get rid of (to eliminate something)
  • Do away with (to abolish or eliminate something)
  • Abandon (to stop using or following something)
Antonyms — Opposite Meanings

• Rely on something
  • Depend on something
  • Stick to something
  • Keep something
  • Maintain something
A Memory Trick

Think of it this way:

"I am dispensing this thing with a wave of my hand — I'm sending it away."

Imagine a queen or king waving their hand and dismissing something from the room. That gesture — removing something from the scene with authority — is exactly what "dispense with" feels like.
Quick Summary

"Dispense with something" means:

  1. To skip or omit something (in the moment)
  2. To permanently get rid of or eliminate something
  3. To dismiss someone from service (formal/polite usage)

In all cases, the core idea is: something is being deliberately removed from the picture, and you are choosing to move forward without it.
